fetched_contents.text: Synergistic Fluoride Adsorption by Composite Adsorbents Synthesized From Different Types of Materials—A Review Abstract The reduction of fluoride concentrations in water is one of many concerns. Adsorption is the most widely used technology for fluoride removal and the center to development of adsorption technology is the improvement of adsorbents. This review classifies the typical fluoride removal adsorbents into four types: metal oxides/hydroxides, biopolymers, carbon-based, and other adsorbents. The exploitation of new materials and the synthesis of composite materials are two ways of developing new adsorbents. In comparison to the discovery of novel adsorbents for fluoride adsorption, research into the composite synthesis of different types of conventional adsorbents has proliferated in recent years. The traditional adsorbents used the earliest, metal oxides, can act as active centers in a wide range of applications for modifying and compounding with other types of adsorbents. This study emphasizes reviewing the research on fluoride removal by composite adsorbents synthesized from different types of metal-modified materials. Seven factors were compared in terms of material characterization, initial fluoride concentration, adsorbent dose, pH, temperature, reaction time, and maximum adsorption capacity. The modification of composite adsorbents is facile and the synergistic effect of the different types of adsorbents significantly improves fluoride adsorption capacity. Metal composite adsorbents are synthesized by facile coprecipitation, hydrothermal, or impregnation modification methods. The adsorption mechanisms involve electrostatic attraction, ion exchange, complexation, and hydrogen bonding. The fluoride adsorption capacity of composite adsorbents has generally improved, indicating that most modifications are successful and have application prospects. However, to achieve significant breakthroughs in practical applications, numerous issues such as cost, separation/regeneration performance, and safety still need to be considered. Low concentrations of fluoride in drinking water (0.5–1.5 mg/L) (Chen et al., 2017) can strengthen bones and prevent dental caries, while excessive concentrations of fluoride (4–10 mg/L) can cause diseases such as fluorosis, osteoporosis, brittle bones, brain damage, and several thyroid disorders (Kumar et al., 2020). Excessive fluoride concentrations in water have become a public health concern in developing countries. High concentration (>10 mg/L) fluorinated wastewater is easier to treat and can be removed or reduced by coagulation, precipitation, electrochemistry, and other methods. The treatment of low concentration (2–10 mg/L) fluorinated wastewater is relatively difficult and is also a current research hotspot. The treatment methods include adsorption (Lin et al., 2016), membrane separation, ion exchange (Xu et al., 2017), nanofiltration (Wang A. et al., 2018), reverse osmosis (Ye et al., 2019), and electrodialysis (Fan et al., 2019). Among them, the adsorption method has the advantages of low cost, high flexibility, simple operation, and high efficiency (Sarkar et al., 2019). It is the most widely used and the treatment effect is more satisfactory. The treatment effectiveness of the adsorption method is influenced by a number of factors, including adsorbent properties, fluoride ion selectivity, compatibility, solution pH, temperature, co-existing ions, and contact time (Pigatto et al., 2020). It mainly depends on the adsorbent properties such as particle size, pore size structure, zero charge point (pH PZC ), and specific surface area (S BET ) (Biswas et al., 2017). High specific surface area (developed pore structure) and ideal chemical surface (abundant functional groups) are two essentials for effective removal of fluoride by adsorbents. Although not systematically categorized, this review found that the main traditional sorbents frequently used for fluoride removal are metal oxides/hydroxides (Dhillon et al., 2017), low-cost carbon materials (Zhang X. et al., 2021), biomolecular materials (Jia et al., 2018), and others such as clay, hydroxyapatite, and graphite. DOI: 10.1039/D6RA00457A (Paper) RSC Adv., 2026, 16, 19779-19801 Received 18th January 2026 , Accepted 21st March 2026 First published on 16th April 2026 ---------------------------------------- Abstract This study reports the development of a sustainable alkali-activated glass-hydroxyapatite composite (AAC-P@HAp) synthesized entirely from waste-derived precursors, including post-consumer glass bottles, eggshells, and plantain bunch stalk ash (as an alkali source), for fluoride removal from aqueous systems. The composite was produced through controlled alkali activation of micronized waste glass followed by hydrothermal-assisted integration of eggshell-derived hydroxyapatite within the aluminosilicate matrix. FTIR, XRF, SEM-EDX, and XRD confirmed successful composite formation of a hybrid silicate-phosphate material and revealed fluoride-induced changes in Ca–P domains after adsorption, indicating strong adsorbent–adsorbate interactions and chemical immobilization. Batch adsorption experiments demonstrated rapid fluoride uptake, with kinetic behavior adequately described by the pseudo-first-order model, while equilibrium data were better represented by the Freundlich isotherm, consistent with heterogeneous surface binding dominated by chemisorption. Thermodynamic analysis indicated that fluoride adsorption was spontaneous and endothermic. Within the Box–Behnken experimental domain, AAC-P@HAp achieved stable fluoride removal efficiencies in a narrow range (83–87%), with pH exerting the dominant influence on performance. Regeneration tests showed good initial reusability followed by a progressive decline attributed to irreversible chemisorption and depletion/phase transformation. In all, the results demonstrate the feasibility of converting multiple waste streams into a robust composite adsorbent and highlights AAC-P@HAp as a circular-economy-oriented material for secure fluoride immobilization rather than extensive multi-cycle reuse. ---------------------------------------- 1. Introduction Fluoride contamination in water sources remains a persistent global concern due to its adverse impacts on human health and ecosystems.1–3 While fluoride is beneficial at trace concentrations, excessive intake through drinking water poses serious health risks and environmental challenges. Consequently, controlling fluoride concentrations in water supplies is a critical issue, particularly in regions that rely heavily on groundwater resources. Fluoride occurs naturally in minerals such as fluorite, fluorapatite, topaz, and cryolite, and geological processes including mineral weathering and dissolution can release fluoride into groundwater, especially in fluoride-rich lithological settings.1,4–7 In addition to geogenic sources, anthropogenic activities such as aluminum smelting, phosphate fertilizer production, coal combustion, and industrial effluent discharge are sources that contribute substantially to environmental fluoride loading.1,8 Chronic consumption of fluoride-contaminated water is strongly associated with dental and skeletal fluorosis, characterized by enamel damage, joint pain, bone stiffness, and skeletal deformities.9 Emerging evidence further indicates potential neurodevelopmental effects. A recent meta-analysis published in JAMA Pediatrics reported a statistically significant association between fluoride exposure and reduced cognitive performance in children, with a decrease of 1.63 IQ points per 1 mg L−1 increase in urinary fluoride.10 Elevated fluoride levels also disrupt metabolic processes in aquatic organisms and impair plant growth, posing risks to both aquatic and terrestrial ecosystems. Globally, fluoride contamination is particularly prevalent in groundwater dependent regions across Africa, Asia, and the Americas, where concentrations frequently exceed the World Health Organization guideline value of 1.5 mg L−1.1 Addressing this challenge is therefore essential for achieving UN Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) 6 (Clean Water and Sanitation) and SDG 3 (Good Health and Well-Being). Among available treatment technologies, adsorption is widely regarded as one of the most practical approaches for fluoride removal due to its operational simplicity, adaptability, and effectiveness over a broad range of water chemistries. However, many conventional fluoride adsorbents suffer from sustainability limitations, which includes high production costs, dependence on virgin raw materials, and environmental burdens associated with synthesis and disposal. These limitations conflict with SDG 12 (responsible consumption and production). In response, growing attention has been directed toward the development of adsorbents derived from waste materials within a circular economy framework. fetched_contents.text: A Review on Adsorption of Fluoride from Aqueous Solution Abstract Fluoride is one of the anionic contaminants which is found in excess in surface or groundwater because of geochemical reactions or anthropogenic activities such as the disposal of industrial wastewaters. Among various methods used for defluoridation of water such as coagulation, precipitation, membrane processes, electrolytic treatment, ion-exchange, the adsorption process is widely used. It offers satisfactory results and seems to be a more attractive method for the removal of fluoride in terms of cost, simplicity of design and operation. Various conventional and non-conventional adsorbents have been assessed for the removal of fluoride from water. In this review, a list of various adsorbents (oxides and hydroxides, biosorbents, geomaterials, carbonaceous materials and industrial products and by-products) and its modifications from literature are surveyed and their adsorption capacities under various conditions are compared. The effect of other impurities on fluoride removal has also been discussed. This survey showed that various adsorbents, especially binary and trimetal oxides and hydroxides, have good potential for the fluoride removal from aquatic environments. Keywords: adsorption, fluoride, adsorbents, fluoride removal, water 1. Introduction Fluorine (F2) is a pale, yellow-green, corrosive gas which almost cannot be found in natural environment in elemental form due to its high electronegativity and reactivity. Fluoride (F−) is a fluorine anion characterized by small radius, great tendency to behave as ligand and easiness to form a great number of different organic and inorganic compounds in soil, rocks, air, plants and animals. Some of those compounds are quite soluble in water, so fluoride is present in surface and groundwater as an almost completely dissociated fluoride ion [1,2]. The presence of naturally occurring fluorides or added fluoridated salts in drinking water allows its easy entrance in the body via the gastrointestinal tract [3,4]. The epidemiological studies reveal that drinking water is the major source of fluoride daily intake and continuous consumption of drinking water with heightened fluoride concentrations (>1.5 mg/L) can induces birth, reproduction and immunological defects [5,6], dental and skeletal fluorosis [7,8,9,10,11,12,13,14]. Besides drinking water, fluoride can also enter into the human body through food, industrial exposure, drugs, cosmetics, etc. [1]. Fluoride occurrence and concentrations in water resources, surface water and groundwater, depends on several contributing factors, such as pH, total dissolved solids, alkalinity, hardness and geochemical composition of aquifers [1,15,16,17,18,19,20], but in many countries worldwide, elevated fluoride concentrations are result of fluorine polluted waste water discharges. Such waste waters are usually produced by the superphosphate fertilizer industry [21,22], glass and ceramic manufacturing processes [23,24], aluminum and zinc smelters [25,26,27], steel production, uranium enrichment facilities, coal fired power stations, beryllium extraction plants, oil refineries [26,28,29,30], photovoltaic solar cells industry [31,32], silicon based high tech-semiconductors production [33,34,35,36] and in municipal waste incineration plants through HF emissions caused by incinerating of fluorinated plastic, fluorinated textiles or CaF2 decomposition in waste sludge [37]. Due to all previously mentioned fluoride pollutions and health problems that it causes, the World Health Organization (WHO) has specified the tolerance limit of fluoride content of drinking water as 1.5 mg/L [38]. Hydroxyapatite-clay composites adsorb fluoride ions through mechanisms that are strongly influenced by water pH. The evidence shows that pH is one of the most critical factors affecting the process efficiency and ionization of the material [N2-R3]. In aqueous systems, fluoride speciation and solubility are pH-dependent: maximum adsorption of fluoride occurred within the pH range of 2–5, while approximately 75% of maximum adsorption was obtained in the pH range of 7–8 [N2-R1]. This indicates that fluoride behavior shifts with pH, with different speciation states likely dominating at acidic, neutral, and basic conditions.

At the surface level, pH affects the availability of reactive sites and surface charge. The review states that the adsorption process is influenced by solution pH, fluoride concentration, temperature, and co-existent ions [N2-R5]. In another source, the adsorbent dosage, initial pollutant level, water pH, and regeneration efficiency were assessed, implying that pH changes can alter the adsorbent’s functional environment [N4-R1]. For hydroxyapatite and related systems, pH also controls surface charge, which determines whether sites are protonated or deprotonated and therefore available for fluoride interaction [N2-R3]. This aligns with the general principle that surface charge state governs site availability for adsorption.

The evidence also highlights competition and hydrolysis effects. In binary-component systems, an increase in equilibrium pH reduced fluoride removal efficiency, and inner-sphere complex formation was observed [N2-R2]. This suggests that higher pH can change the speciation of fluoride itself and promote competing inner-sphere complexes, which may outcompete fluoride for adsorption sites. Similarly, the review notes that co-existent ions and other impurities play a major role in controlling fluoride adsorption [N2-R5], which means pH changes can indirectly affect competing ions’ speciation and their ability to interfere with fluoride uptake.

Overall, pH influences fluoride adsorption and speciation by altering fluoride speciation and solubility, changing surface charge and site availability, and introducing competition from other ions or hydrolysis products [N2-R1][N2-R2][N2-R3][N2-R5]. The most direct evidence here is the review evidence [N2-F3] and the related search evidence [N2-R1][N2-R2][N2-R3][N2-R5].

## How hydroxyapatite-clay composites adsorb fluoride ions

Hydroxyapatite-clay composites adsorb fluoride ions through a combination of specific adsorption sites, reactive bonding modes, and synergy between the hydroxyapatite and clay components. The direct evidence shows that hydroxyapatite is well known for its strong affinity toward fluoride ions because of its calcium- and phosphate-rich structure [N1-R2], and that adsorption mechanisms often involve electrostatic attraction, ion exchange, complexation, and hydrogen bonding [N1-F1]. This means fluoride binding is not limited to a single mode but is instead a multi-faceted process.

### Specific adsorption sites and bonding modes

The composite surface contains reactive centers and functional groups that contribute to fluoride uptake. The evidence indicates that hydroxyapatite/clay nanocomposites have reactive centers such as Al–Al–OH, Si–Si, and other surface groups, as revealed by FT-IR analysis [N3-R1][N6-R1]. In hydroxyapatite-cellulose composites, hydroxyapatite effectively adsorbs fluoride through ion exchange [N6-R3], which is one of the bonding modes described in the general adsorption mechanism [N1-F1]. These reactive sites provide the physical and chemical basis for fluoride interaction, while the composite structure allows multiple bonding modes to coexist.

### Role of hydroxyapatite and clay in enhancing uptake

Hydroxyapatite provides the primary fluoride-binding framework, while clay contributes additional reactive surface centers and can sorb cations and, to a lesser extent, anions without significantly affecting the crystal structure [N3-R2][N1-R2]. The composite structure enhances uptake by increasing surface area, introducing additional reactive sites, and modulating the overall surface chemistry [N3-R1][N3-R2]. The evidence also emphasizes that high specific surface area and ideal chemical surface with abundant functional groups are two essentials for effective fluoride removal [N1-F1]. This makes the composite more efficient than either component alone, because hydroxyapatite offers strong fluoride affinity and clay improves surface reactivity and site availability.

### Kinetic and thermodynamic factors that control adsorption

Kinetic and thermodynamic factors are central to the adsorption behavior. The review notes that treatment effectiveness depends on pH, temperature, co-existing ions, contact time, and other operating conditions [N1-F1]. The thermodynamics evidence indicates that fluoride adsorption can be spontaneous and endothermic [N1-F2], which means adsorption is more favorable at higher temperatures and can proceed without a significant energy barrier. At the same time, the kinetics evidence shows that adsorption rates can increase with stirring rate and pH [N2-R4]. These findings suggest that temperature, pH, and contact time are important kinetic controls, while thermodynamic factors determine whether adsorption is energetically favorable under different conditions [N1-F1][N1-F2][N2-R4]. Together, these factors explain why adsorption performance can vary significantly with operating conditions and why composite design must balance multiple physicochemical properties [N1-F1][N1-F2].

## How water pH affects fluoride adsorption and speciation

Water pH strongly influences fluoride adsorption and speciation. The evidence shows that pH is one of the most critical factors affecting the process efficiency and ionization of the material [N2-R3]. In aqueous systems, fluoride speciation and solubility are pH-dependent: maximum adsorption of fluoride occurred within the pH range of 2–5, while approximately 75% of maximum adsorption was obtained in the pH range of 7–8 [N2-R1]. This indicates that fluoride behavior shifts with pH, with different speciation states likely dominating at acidic, neutral, and basic conditions.

### pH influences fluoride speciation and solubility

At lower pH, fluoride is more likely to remain in solution as F⁻, whereas at higher pH, it may hydrolyze or form species such as HF, HF₂⁻, and other species that can compete with fluoride adsorption [N2-R1][N2-R3]. The review also notes that pH controls surface charge and site availability, which is important because it determines whether reactive sites on the adsorbent are protonated or deprotonated and therefore accessible [N2-R3]. This means that pH changes can alter the speciation of fluoride itself and the speciation of the adsorbent surface, both of which affect binding.

### pH-dependent surface charge and site availability

The evidence indicates that pH changes alter surface charge and thus affect site availability. The review states that solution pH, fluoride concentration, temperature, and co-existent ions play a major role in controlling fluoride adsorption onto soil adsorbents [N2-R5]. In hydroxyapatite and related systems, pH also controls surface charge, which determines whether sites are protonated or deprotonated and therefore available for fluoride interaction [N2-R3]. This is consistent with the general principle that surface charge state governs site availability for adsorption.

### Competition from other ions or hydrolysis products

Higher pH can also introduce competition from other ions or hydrolysis products. In binary-component systems, an increase in equilibrium pH reduced fluoride removal efficiency, and inner-sphere complex formation was observed [N2-R2]. This suggests that higher pH can change the speciation of fluoride itself and promote competing inner-sphere complexes, which may outcompete fluoride for adsorption sites. The review further notes that co-existent ions and other impurities play a major role in controlling fluoride adsorption [N2-R5], meaning pH changes can indirectly affect competing ions’ speciation and their ability to interfere with fluoride uptake.

## Challenges from pH changes during adsorption and regeneration

This suggests that higher pH can change the speciation of fluoride itself and promote competing inner-sphere complexes, which may outcompete fluoride for adsorption sites. The review further notes that co-existent ions and other impurities play a major role in controlling fluoride adsorption [N2-R5], meaning pH changes can indirectly affect competing ions’ speciation and their ability to interfere with fluoride uptake.

## Challenges from pH changes during adsorption and regeneration

Changes in water pH during adsorption and regeneration present several important challenges for hydroxyapatite-clay composites. One of the most direct challenges is structural and surface degradation under extreme pH. The evidence shows that the adsorbent dosage, initial pollutant level, water pH, and regeneration efficiency were assessed, and fluoride ion adsorption was affected [N4-R1]. In bone char studies, the fluoride adsorption capacity decreased substantially with increasing pH from 3.0 to 11.0 [N4-R3], which implies that pH changes can directly impair adsorption performance. This is especially concerning for composites where hydroxyapatite and clay together provide reactive sites; a shift in pH can alter the surface environment in ways that reduce available binding sites.

### Regeneration efficiency and desorption behavior

Regeneration efficiency is also challenged by pH changes. The regeneration of adsorbents exhausted by fluoride was accomplished by creating new Al-based active sites on the surfaces of fluoride-saturated adsorbents [N4-R2]. This implies that regeneration is not a simple reversal of adsorption but requires active site recovery, which may be compromised by irreversible changes under extreme pH. In the same evidence base, regeneration tests showed good initial reusability followed by a progressive decline attributed to irreversible chemisorption and depletion/phase transformation [N4-F4]. This directly supports the challenge of pH-induced irreversible changes during regeneration.

### Practical operational constraints in real water systems

Practical operational constraints in real water systems are evident from the evidence on pH dependence and regeneration. The review emphasizes that pH is one of the most critical factors affecting the process efficiency and ionization of the material [N2-R3], while another source notes that co-existent ions and other impurities play a major role in controlling fluoride adsorption [N2-R5]. In real water treatment, pH will rarely remain constant, so adsorbents must be designed to tolerate a range of conditions. However, the evidence also shows that regeneration is sensitive to irreversible changes [N4-F4], meaning that real-world systems face both adsorption performance limits and regeneration limitations when pH fluctuates.

## How surface functionalization and clay interaction affect adsorption behavior

Surface functionalization and clay interaction significantly affect the adsorption behavior of hydroxyapatite/clay composites. The evidence shows that hydroxyapatite/clay nanocomposites have reactive centers such as Al–Al–OH, Si–Si, and other functional groups [N3-R1][N6-R1]. This means the composite surface is not inert but has specific reactive sites that can interact with fluoride and other ions. The clay’s role is particularly important because clay can sorb cations and, to a lesser extent, anions without significantly affecting the crystal structure, with exchangeable ions attracted by the surface [N3-R2]. This is a key point: the clay contributes to adsorption through surface exchange and cation-anion interactions, which can complement or modify the hydroxyapatite-dominated binding mechanism [N3-R2].

### Cation-anion exchange and ion pairing effects

Cation-anion exchange and ion pairing effects are explicitly supported by the evidence. The general adsorption mechanisms include ion exchange, electrostatic attraction, complexation, and hydrogen bonding [N1-F1]. In hydroxyapatite-cellulose composites, fluoride is adsorbed through ion exchange [N6-R3], which directly supports the idea that ion exchange is a major mechanism. The clay evidence also suggests that exchangeable cations can be attracted to the surface [N3-R2], implying that cation-anion exchange and ion pairing effects are relevant for the composite’s overall adsorption behavior. In other words, the composite is not just a passive support for hydroxyapatite; the clay can mediate additional ion exchange processes that enhance fluoride uptake [N3-R2][N6-R3].

### How composite structure influences fluoride uptake

The composite structure influences fluoride uptake by creating a heterogeneous and reactive surface environment. The review emphasizes that high specific surface area and ideal chemical surface with abundant functional groups are two essentials for effective fluoride removal [N1-F1]. The evidence also shows that reactive centers and functional groups are present on both hydroxyapatite and clay [N3-R1][N6-R1]. This means the composite structure enhances uptake by increasing the number of available binding sites and by introducing surface groups that can participate in fluoride adsorption. The composite’s heterogeneous binding behavior is consistent with adsorption models such as pseudo-first-order and Freundlich isotherms, which are often associated with heterogeneous surface binding [N1-F2]. Overall, the surface functionalization and clay interaction work together to improve adsorption behavior by increasing site density, altering surface charge, and enabling multiple bonding modes [N3-R1][N3-R2][N6-R1][N6-R3][N1-F1].

## Integrated conclusion

In summary, hydroxyapatite-clay composites adsorb fluoride ions through a combination of specific adsorption sites, reactive bonding modes, and synergy between hydroxyapatite and clay. Hydroxyapatite provides strong fluoride affinity, while clay contributes reactive surface centers and can mediate cation-anion exchange and ion pairing effects [N1-R2][N1-F1][N3-R2][N6-R3]. Kinetic and thermodynamic factors such as temperature, pH, and contact time also control adsorption, with adsorption often being spontaneous and endothermic [N1-F1][N1-F2]. However, changes in water pH during adsorption and regeneration pose significant challenges. pH can alter fluoride speciation and solubility, change surface charge and site availability, and introduce competition from other ions or hydrolysis products [N2-R1][N2-R2][N2-R3][N2-R5]. Extreme pH can degrade structural and surface properties, reduce regeneration efficiency, and produce irreversible changes such as depletion or phase transformation [N4-R3][N4-R2][N4-F4]. In real water systems, this means adsorbents must be designed to handle a range of pH conditions while maintaining long-term performance and regeneration capability [N2-R3][N2-R5][N4-F4].

Overall, hydroxyapatite-clay composites offer a promising approach for fluoride removal because they combine the strong fluoride affinity of hydroxyapatite with the reactive and functional properties of clay [N1-R2][N3-R2][N6-R1]. But their practical success depends on careful control of pH and on the ability to withstand pH-induced changes during adsorption and regeneration [N2-R3][N4-F4][N4-R3].
